Among them are those who do not menstruate even when they reach puberty, and among them are those who menstruate very lightly, with the gap between their periods (al-qur', the menstrual cycles) widening until they menstruate once a year. For this reason the scholars agreed that there is no limit to the maximum length of purity between two menstrual periods. Most women menstruate once a month, bleed for about a quarter of the month, and their purity is three-quarters of it. Among them are women who remain pure for several months because their moisture is little, and among them are those in whom dryness comes quickly, so their menstruation stops and they despair of it, even if they are under fifty, or even forty. Among them are those in whom dryness does not come quickly, so they pass fifty while still menstruating. He said: There is nothing in the Book or the Sunnah that fixes the time of despair (al-yaʾs) to a particular age. Had the intended meaning of "those who have despaired of menstruation" been those who are fifty years old, or sixty, or otherwise, it would have been said, "and those who reach such-and-such an age," and it would not have said "who have despaired."

Also, it is firmly established from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that they considered whoever's menstruation had stopped before that age to be one who has despaired, as has already been mentioned. The actual situation varies regarding the time of their despair and is not uniform. Moreover, Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And those who have despaired﴾, and if it had a fixed time, women and others would be equal in knowing their despair. Yet He, glorified is He, singled out women by saying they are the ones who have despaired, just as He singled them out with His words ﴿and those who have not menstruated﴾. So the one who menstruates is the one who despairs. This is different from doubt (al-irtiyab), for He, glorified is He, said ﴿if you doubt﴾ and did not say "if they doubt." That is, if you doubt their ruling and are uncertain about it, then this is the view—not that. This is what the majority of the people of tafsir (exegesis) hold, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his Tafsir from the hadith of Jarir and Musa ibn A'yan, the wording being his, from Mutarrif ibn Tarif, from Amr ibn Salim, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, some people in Madinah say about the numbers of women what Allah has not mentioned in the Qur'an: the young, the old, and the pregnant.' So Allah, glorified is He, revealed in this surah: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you have doubt, their waiting period is three months, and those who have not menstruated; and for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth﴾."

So the term of each of them is that she gives birth to her burden. When she gives birth, she has completed her waiting period.

The wording of Jarir is: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, some people of Madinah, when this verse in al-Baqarah about the waiting period of women was revealed, said: there remain among the numbers of women some numbers not mentioned in the Qur'an: the young and the old whose menstruation has ceased, and women who are pregnant.' He said: So the shorter one among women was revealed: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you have doubt﴾." Then it was narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His words: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation﴾, meaning the aged woman who does not menstruate, or the woman who has ceased from the menstrual period—these are not among the periods (qur') in anything.

As for His words in the verse ﴿if you doubt﴾, meaning: if you are in doubt, then their waiting period is three months. And from Mujahid: "If you doubt" means if you do not know the waiting period of the woman who has ceased menstruating, or the one who has not menstruated, ﴿then their waiting period is three months﴾.

So His words, exalted is He, ﴿if you doubt﴾ mean: if you ask about their ruling and do not know their ruling and are uncertain about it, then We have explained it to you. It is thus a clarification of His blessing upon the one who seeks knowledge of it, so that the doubt and uncertainty he has may be removed, in contrast to the one who turns away from seeking knowledge. Moreover, women do not share the same onset of menstruation; some menstruate at ten, or twelve, or fifteen, or more than that. Likewise, they do not share the same last age of menstruation, which is the age of despair, and experience bears witness to this. Moreover, they have disputed regarding a woman who has reached puberty but has not menstruated: does she observe a waiting period of three months, or a year, like the woman whose menstruation has stopped and who does not know what removed it? On this there are two reports from Ahmad.

I say: The majority hold that she observes a waiting period of three months, and they did not set a limit to the youth that makes the waiting period obligatory. Likewise, it must be that there is no limit to the old age that makes the waiting period in months obligatory. This is evident, and to Allah belongs all praise.

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some preceding discussion:

If it is said: There remains one matter against you, namely that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Lodge them where you dwell, according to your means﴾ refers only to the irrevocably divorced (al-bawa'in), not to the revocably divorced (al-raj'iyyat), as evidenced by His saying right after it: ﴿And do not harm them in order to restrict them. And if they are pregnant, then spend on them until they give birth to their load﴾.

This applies to the irrevocably divorced woman, for if she were revocable, the stipulation of maintenance for her by pregnancy would not have been specified, and it would have been ineffective, since she is entitled to it whether she is non-pregnant or pregnant. And the apparent reading is that the pronoun in "lodge them" and the pronoun in His saying ﴿And if they are pregnant, then spend on them﴾ refer to the same group.

The answer is: the one raising this question is either (1) among those who make maintenance and lodging obligatory, or (2) among those who make only lodging obligatory without maintenance. If he is the first, then the verse is a proof against him according to his own view, because He, glorified is He, made the obligation of maintenance for them conditional upon their being pregnant, and a ruling attached to a condition is negated when the condition is negated. Thus it indicates that the irrevocably divorced non-pregnant woman has no maintenance.

If it is said: This is an indication through mafhum (implicit meaning), and they do not hold by it.

It is said: This is not from the indication of mafhum, but from the negation of the ruling when its condition is negated; for if the ruling remained after its negation, the condition would not be a condition.

If he is among those who make only lodging obligatory, it is said to him: There is not a single pronoun in the verse that is specific to the irrevocably divorced. Rather, its pronouns are of two types: a type that is definitely specific to the revocably divorced, such as His saying ﴿So when they have reached their term, either retain them in good manner or part from them in good manner﴾;

and a type that may refer to the irrevocably divorced, or to the revocably divorced, or to both, which is His saying ﴿Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave﴾,

and His saying ﴿Lodge them where you dwell, according to your means﴾.

So interpreting it as referring to the revocably divorced is the required reading, so that the pronouns and their referent are unified. If it were read as referring to other than them, there would be a mismatch between the pronouns and their referent, which contradicts the original principle, and reading according to the original principle is preferable.

If it is said: What is the benefit of restricting the maintenance of the revocably divorced to her being pregnant?

It is said: The verse does not imply that there is no maintenance for the non-pregnant revocably divorced woman. Rather, revocably divorced women are of two types, whose rulings Allah has explained in His Book: a non-pregnant one, for whom maintenance is due by the marriage contract, since her ruling is the ruling of wives; or a pregnant one, for whom maintenance is due by this verse until she gives birth to her load. After birth, the maintenance becomes the maintenance of a relative, not the maintenance of a husband. Thus her state before giving birth differs from her state after it, for the husband spends on her alone while she is pregnant; once she has given birth, her maintenance falls upon the one obligated to maintain the child. Her state during pregnancy is not such that her maintenance falls upon the one obligated to maintain the child, since during pregnancy the fetus is a part of her; once separated, it has a different ruling, and the maintenance shifts from one ruling to another. Thus the benefit of the restriction and the wisdom of the condition become apparent. And Allah knows best what He intended by His speech.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 65, verse 12:

He informs us that He created the world so that His servants would know the perfection of His power and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and this entails knowing Him, knowing His names and attributes, and affirming His oneness (tawhid).

(A benefit)

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, was asked about the interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾.

He said to the questioner: "What assurance do you have that, if I informed you of it, you would not disbelieve?" ... meaning: if I informed you of its interpretation, you would disbelieve in it, and your disbelief in it would be your denial of it.

Thus, a subtle and delicate matter that is given to those who are not its people is like a beautiful woman who is presented to a blind, paralyzed man, as it has been said:

A bride being escorted to a blind, paralyzed man.

And when some disturbance occurred during the course of Abu ʿAli's gathering, he would say: "This is from the jealousy of the Truth," meaning that what happens of the clouding of the moment should not occur.

(Section: the plural of "sama" (heaven) and its derivation)

If you say: Why did they pluralize "sama" and say "samawat," and why did they not observe in it what they observed in "ard" (earth), since they are counterparts? What is the difference between them?

It is said: There are two differences, a verbal difference and a semantic difference.

As for the verbal one: "ard" (ard) is on the pattern of the three-letter verbal nouns, and it is of the form faʿl, like ḍarb.

As for "samawat": its counterpart among the verbal nouns would be talaʾ and jalaʾ, so it resembles the patterns of nouns more closely. What corresponds to "ard" in meaning and pattern are "sufl" (lower) and "taht" (under), and neither of these is dualized or pluralized; and opposite them are "fawq" (above) and "ʿulu" (height), which likewise are not pluralized.

Moreover, it has been said that "samawat" is not the plural of "sama," but the plural of "samawa," and the "samawa" of a thing is its uppermost part. But the plural of "sama" by analogy would be "asmiya," like "akhsiya" and "aghtiya," or "samawat." This is nothing, for "samawa" specifically denotes the highest part of a thing, and is not a name for a lofty thing in general; it is the name of its high part only.

As for "sama," it is the name of this raised ceiling in its entirety, so "samawat" is its plural, not the plural of high parts of it, on the basis that everything high is a "sama."

A better explanation than this is that if they had pluralized "ard" according to the analogy of broken plurals, they would have said "aaraḍ" like "aflus," or "araḍ" like "ajmal," or "urud" like "fulus." They found this form heavy, since it lacks the eloquence, beauty and sweetness that the word "samawat" has, and you find the ear recoils from it to the same degree that it finds the word "samawat" pleasing. The word "samawat" enters the ear without asking permission, because of its clarity and sweetness, whereas the word "aradi" is not admitted by the ear except with reluctance. For this reason they avoided pluralizing it when they wished to, using three words that indicate multiplicity, as the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾.

All of this to avoid saying "arad" or "araḍ."

The semantic difference: when speech focuses on the sensible sky, which is the ceiling, and intends its very essence rather than the meaning of description, its plural is correctly the sound plural (jamʿ al-salamah), because the number is small, and the sound plural is more appropriate for a small number, given its closeness to the dual, which is close to the singular. But when speech focuses on the description and the meaning of height and exaltation, the word is treated like the verbal noun described by it, as in your saying: "qawl ʿadul" and "zawr."

As for "ard," it most often comes with the intended meaning of "under" and "lower," without intending its essence and its number. Where it comes with the intended meaning of essence and number, it is expressed with a word indicating distance, as in His saying: ﴿and of the earth the like thereof﴾.

The second difference is that the earth has a proportion not in relation to the heavens and their vastness; rather, compared to them it is like a pebble in a desert. So though it is multiplied and enlarged, in relation to the heaven it is like a small single unit, and therefore the generic noun was chosen for it.

The third difference is that the earth is the abode of this world, which, compared to the Hereafter, is like a person dipping his finger into the sea; what is connected to it is a sample of the Hereafter from this world. Allah, glorified is He, mentions the world only to diminish it and belittle its status. As for the heavens, they are not of this world, according to one of the two opinions on the meaning of "dunya," since it is a name for a place. The heavens are the abode of the angels of the Lord, the place of His recompense, and the descent point of His angels and His revelation. So when the expression intends their essence, it is expressed with the plural form, since the intent is their essences and not merely height and above-ness.

But when the comprehensive description of the heavens is intended, namely the meaning of height and above-ness, they are expressed in the singular according to what the speech and context connect it to. Reflect on His saying: ﴿Do you feel secure from He who is in the sky that He will cause the earth to swallow you, and behold, it shakes? (16) Or do you feel secure from He who is in the sky that He will send against you a storm of stones?﴾

How it is singular here: because the intended meaning is the comprehensive description and absolute above-ness, and not a specific, particular sky.

And since the Jahmiyyah did not grasp this meaning, they proceeded to distort the verse from its places.
